page: Amazon Web Services c7i-flex.8xlarge is a compute-optimized instance powered by a 3.2 GHz Intel Xeon 8488C processor built on the x86_64 architecture and managed by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. The virtual machine provides 32 vCPUs across 16 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading, alongside 105 MB of L3 cache. It is equipped with 64 GB of DDR5 memory clocked at 5000 MHz, yielding a compute-to-memory ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. Hardware instruction support includes Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), AVX-512, and accelerated cryptographic features. The instance contains no bundled local storage and operates with a baseline network bandwidth of 6 Gbps without dedicated GPUs.

Benchmark evaluations reveal strong results in single-core and multi-core processing, with Geekbench scores of 2074.0 and 15951.0 placing the instance within the top quartile. Single-threaded data compression and decompression reach 33.6 GB/sec for gzip and 13.85 GB/sec for bzip3, while static web serving throughput measures at 51.12 GB/sec. Memory bandwidth benchmarks and sustained multi-core stress tests land in the average tier, consistent with the burstable CPU allocation profile of the Flex family.

The burstable CPU model makes this configuration a cost-efficient alternative to fixed-performance compute instances when steady peak CPU utilization is not continuously required. Tradeoffs include the lack of local NVMe storage and burstable CPU constraints under persistent load. This hardware footprint is suited for web serving fleets, continuous integration pipelines, batch data compression, and lightweight machine learning inference utilizing AMX extensions.
description: Amazon Web Services c7i-flex.8xlarge is a compute-optimized instance running on the AWS Nitro hypervisor and powered by an Intel Xeon 8488C processor at 3.2 GHz. Using an x86_64 architecture with burstable CPU allocation, it supplies 32 vCPUs across 16 physical cores, supported by 105 MB of L3 cache and 64 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory. The instance does not feature local storage or discrete GPUs, relying on remote block volumes and providing 6 Gbps of baseline network throughput. Benchmark testing demonstrates strong performance in single-core operations, data compression, cryptographic tasks, and static web serving, with PassMark CPU scoring in the top quartile. The instance balances modern compute performance with resource-dense cost efficiency, making it well matched for web serving tiers, continuous integration pipelines, microservices, and CPU-based inference tasks.
